checks.finding: The source's legibility is checkability, where a verifier accepts the helpful prover's correct solutions and cannot be fooled by convincing incorrect ones; Baker et al. turn it into the monitor's belief that the latent carries useful information about v, a belief-based test that convincing sneaky solutions would pass but the source's soundness condition rules out.
checks.source_evidence: When we find helpful provers and verifiers with such limited completeness and soundness properties, we say that the helpful prover is legible to the verifier. This is analogous to saying that outputs are legible to humans if humans accept them as correct and can’t be fooled by similar-looking incorrect outputs.
checks.citing_evidence: The latent is plausible (P) or legible if the monitor believes it is getting useful information about $v$ from the latent.

checks.finding: The source defines legibility relative to a particular verifier (checkability of solution correctness by that verifier or by humans); Baker et al. carry over the observer-relative notion but use it as a monitor's ability to read the latent at all (e.g. French CoT, English-only monitor), separate from faithfulness.
checks.source_evidence: One possible way to gain trust in the output of a complex system is to require that the system produces an explanation of its output that is legible to humans or another trusted system, i.e. can be fully understood to the extend that any possible errors would be spotted. [...] When we find helpful provers and verifiers with such limited completeness and soundness properties, we say that the helpful prover is legible to the verifier.
checks.citing_evidence: We further have viewed lack of legibility [74] or plausibility [27] as another failure mode of monitorability. If we assume that an agent’s latent is faithful with respect to a $v$ , an observable property of its behavior, then a monitor can only succeed if that latent is legible to the monitor. For instance, if an agent’s CoT tokens are in French but the monitor only understands English, the monitor will fail due to illegibility.

checks.finding: The source defines legibility as reasoning that is clear and easy to check and says it requires outputs that are coherent and accessible to human understanding, which is the 'understandable by humans' requirement Chen et al. attribute to it.
checks.source_evidence: One way to increase confidence in the outputs of Large Language Models (LLMs) is to support them with reasoning that is clear and easy to check — a property we call legibility. [...] Consequently, legibility requires model outputs that are coherent and accessible to human understanding (Rudin, 2019).
checks.citing_evidence: For CoT monitoring to be most effective, the CoT must be a legible and faithful reflection of the way the model reached its conclusion and generated the user-facing response. This means that the model’s CoT must be understandable by humans (Kirchner et al., 2024)

checks.finding: The source defines checkability as a verifier's capacity to check the correctness of a prover's solutions and calls a prover legible to a verifier when completeness and soundness hold, i.e. legibility operationalised as checkability by a designated verifier.
checks.source_evidence: Checkability — i.e. the capacity of a verifier to independently check the correctness of solutions generated by a helpful prover — can be defined by a combination of two properties: [...] When we find helpful provers and verifiers with such limited completeness and soundness properties, we say that the helpful prover is legible to the verifier.
checks.citing_evidence: Prover–verifier games train for solution checkability by a learned verifier (Kirchner et al., 2024). These approaches are complementary to tandem training. Specification-based methods are well suited when a target behavior is available, while prover–verifier methods operationalize legibility as checkability by a designated verifier.

checks.finding: The source measures human legibility as the accuracy of time-limited humans judging solution correctness; Jose et al. replace this with a GPT-4o grader rating legibility on a 1–9 scale, saying so explicitly.
checks.source_evidence: In this work we measured human legibility via the accuracy of their judgement of solution correctness in time-limited settings, which is only one of many ways to measure human legibility.
checks.citing_evidence: (Kirchner et al., 2024) measures legibility using time-constrained human contractors. So, we use a weaker "trusted" model as our autograder (Greenblatt et al., 2024b); [...] We prompt GPT-4o to evaluate the CoTs for legibility on a scale of 1-9, with 1 being the most legible and 9 the least.

checks.finding: The source reports that the checkability-trained prover has lower accuracy than the correctness-only prover and names this a legibility tax, a term it credits to Leike (2022).
checks.source_evidence: It has lower test performance than the prover optimized for correctness alone, which represents an instance of a legibility tax (Leike, 2022).
checks.citing_evidence: Prover-verifier games can be used to improve checkability of model outputs, but display a degradation in accuracy compared to a baseline trained only to maximize correctness—a phenonemon called legibility tax (Kirchner et al., 2024).

checks.finding: The source's completeness requires the prover to be always correct and accepted, and its soundness quantifies over adversarial provers of the same model family; Kim et al. move correctness out into a separate condition (completeness becomes correct ⇒ accepted) and quantify soundness over every possible proof z′, as they state when 'decoupling correctness from the definition of checkability'.

checks.finding: The source supports the soundness half (a smaller verifier rejecting incorrect solutions from sneaky provers) but not the claim that this defines legibility: the source calls a prover legible only when completeness also holds, i.e. the verifier accepts the helpful prover's correct solutions.

The verifier rejects all incorrect solutions produced by any adversarial provers of the same model class as the helpful one. [...] When we find helpful provers and verifiers with such limited completeness and soundness properties, we say that the helpful prover is legible to the verifier.

checks.finding: The source's prover-verifier game trains a smaller verifier against helpful and sneaky roles of a larger prover on whole CoT solutions; Roytburg et al. move it to intermediate reasoning traces and make it non-adversarial, as they state.
checks.source_evidence: Our algorithm iteratively trains small verifiers to predict solution correctness, “helpful” provers to produce correct solutions that the verifier accepts, and “sneaky” provers to produce incorrect solutions that fool the verifier.
checks.citing_evidence: Kirchner et al. (2024) defines legibility with a prover-verifier game, where a weak verifier must learn to invalidate responses from a stronger, misaligned prover. We extend this setup to intermediate reasoning traces and reframe it as a non-adversarial interaction, enabling connections between legibility for safety and for distillation, caching, and re-use.

checks.finding: Madsen et al. do not run a simulatability evaluation: they measure faithfulness with self-consistency checks that re-run the model on its own explanation-edited input, and explicitly set this apart from simulatability (an observer predicting the model's behaviour), which they attribute to Chen et al. [...] A challenge with simulatability is it’s difficult to ensure that humans use the explanations and not their world-knowledge to predict the model. checks.finding: The source has the model itself generate the counterfactual (an edit meant to yield the opposite label) instead of a separate explainer, which is the self-generated counterfactual explanation Dehghanighobadi et al. say Madsen et al. also evaluate.

For each style, we then edit the inputs according to the generated self-explanations and compute faithfulness as the proportion of cases in which the model’s prediction changes. We exclude instances that violate either the style condition or the number-of-word condition

checks.finding: The source's attribution check replaces the listed words with [REDACTED] and counts the explanation faithful only if the model can no longer classify the input (it must be allowed to answer 'unknown'); Doi et al. keep the [REDACTED] replacement but count any change of prediction.
checks.source_evidence: The model response is a list of important words, and the matching words in the paragraph are replaced with “[REDACTED]”. [...] Given a faithful explanation, it will be impossible for the model to perform the classification task (Samek et al., 2017; Hooker et al., 2019; Madsen et al., 2022a), assuming that the model understands the meaning of redaction/masking during classification.
checks.citing_evidence: If the explanation is faithful, the listed words should have a substantial impact on the prediction being explained. Faithfulness is therefore assessed by examining whether the prediction changes when the listed words are removed from the original input. Following Madsen et al. (2024), we create such redacted inputs by automatically replacing the listed input words with the “[REDACTED]” tokens rather than deleting them, in order to preserve the grammatical structure.

checks.finding: The source's redaction explanation is the model's own [REDACTED] copy of the input, faithful only if the model then cannot classify it; Doi et al. keep the model-made redaction but count any prediction change as faithful.
checks.source_evidence: Instead of algorithmically replacing important words with “[REDACTED]”, we ask the model to perform the replacement directly. [...] Besides the different replacement mechanisms, the interpretability-faithfulness metric works the same. The explanation is faithful if the model can not classify the redacted paragraph.
checks.citing_evidence: Redaction In this style, the model directly generates a redacted version of the input in which the words it deems important for its prediction are replaced with “[REDACTED]”. [...] We evaluate faithfulness by checking whether the model’s prediction changes when it is given the redacted input sentence it produced.

checks.finding: The source's counterfactual is the model's edit of the input toward the opposite label, faithful if re-evaluation gives that label; Doi et al. add editing-distance constraints set in the prompt (one word by default), which the source does not impose.
checks.source_evidence: Counterfactuals are explanations where the input is modified such that the model predicts the opposite label. [...] Because the goal is to produce the opposite label, we can re-evaluate the prediction with the counterfactual and check that this goal is satisfied. If satisfied, the counterfactual is faithful.
checks.citing_evidence: Counterfactual This style requires the model to edit the input sentence such that the resulting sentence changes the model’s original prediction. The model may add, remove, or replace input words, subject to editing-distance constraints specified in a prompt. To evaluate faithfulness, we feed the generated counterfactual sentences back into the model and test whether the predicted label changes accordingly.

checks.finding: The source supports that LLM self-explanations are often unfaithful and can create unsupported confidence, but not this claim about reasoning chains: it tests only counterfactual, feature-attribution and redaction explanations and evaluates no chain-of-thought.
checks.source_evidence: However, convincing and wrong self-explanations can lead to unsupported confidence in LLMs, thus increasing risk. Therefore, it’s important to measure if self-explanations truly reflect the model’s behavior.
